headline: Trump's new chief of staff wrote the immigration policy.
summary: Susie Wiles resigned as White House chief of staff Thursday night, two days after Republicans lost both houses of Congress. Trump gave the job to Stephen Miller, 41, who wrote his immigration crackdown, from Monday. He said Wiles had "done a very good job" but "we've got to make moves sometimes." She was the first woman in the job.

cover_question.q: What does a chief of staff do?

cover_answer: Guards the president's door. From Monday, that's Miller.
table_question: If your plan lost the vote, would you change it or push harder?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president has a helper who runs his office and decides who gets in to see him, like the person at the front desk at school. Susie Wiles had that job, and she quit this week. On Monday a man named Stephen Miller starts in it. Nothing changes for you.
5-7.why: One helper leaves, one arrives, and the front desk is a place they walk past every morning. The job is the desk; the politics can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the job becomes the front desk at school and the news is one person leaving and one arriving on Monday. Nothing here needs an election or a policy. Expect "did he fire her?" She quit, and the president said she did a very good job. That is the whole story at this age.

8-12.script: The chief of staff is the president's gatekeeper: who gets in, who deals with Congress. Tuesday, Trump's party lost Congress. Thursday night Susie Wiles quit; Axios says Trump blamed her. Friday he gave the gate to Stephen Miller, who wrote the immigration rules a poll says went too far.
8-12.why: Gate, loss, blame, new gatekeeper: a chain, then a fairness call.
8-12.why_long: At this age they are working out cause and effect and whether blame lands where it should, so the script hands over the chain: a lost election, a resignation two days later, a replacement who wrote the rules voters just rejected. Expect "was it her fault?" Trump blamed her, Axios says. Let them argue it.

13-17.script: Democrats run Congress from January, and the chief of staff is the president's negotiator with them. Their leader, Hakeem Jeffries, calls Stephen Miller "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist." Can those two make a deal? Second: Miller calls the job a fight. Is a fighter the right hire for deals?
13-17.why: Two true things: a job built on deals, and a hire who promises a fight.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the job is built on negotiating with Congress, and the man now in it calls his mission a fight. The script sets Jeffries' words against Miller's. Expect "doesn't he have to listen to the vote?" No law says so, and Trump says he will work with Democrats. Ask what that is worth.

5-7.a: No. She quit this week, after his team lost a big vote. He said she did a very good job.

8-12.q: What does a chief of staff do?
8-12.a: Decides who gets in to see the president, and who deals with Congress.

8-12.q: Why would she quit if she did a good job?
8-12.a: Her party lost. Axios says Trump blamed her, not himself.

13-17.q: Can Miller work with people who call him that?
13-17.a: He has to try. A Trump adviser told Axios he's 'a wartime adviser'.

13-17.q: Didn't voters just reject his policies?
13-17.a: A poll found 58% said enforcement went too far. Trump promoted its author.
